text: Exhibition HUMANITARIAN, BY DESIGN? Geneva. October 8 – August 29, 2026 Humanitarian, by Design? Le design au cœur de l’humanitaire explores the objects commonly used in humanitarian action – such as first-aid kits, tents, prostheses, maps and makeshift shelters – and asks what they reveal about the lives of those who rely on them. The exhibition examines how design – whether improvised, institutional or repurposed – shapes life in situations of crisis, displacement or extreme precarity. From hacked plastics to architectures of waiting, and from personal stories to crisis imagery, it sheds light on fragile and often invisible practices designed for purposes of endurance, resistance and hope. The exhibition was developed through a collaboration between HEAD – Genève, the Geneva Graduate Institute, the University of Copenhagen, the EPFL EssentialTech Centre and the International Red Cross and Red Crescent Museum. Humanitarian, by Design? is structured around three interconnected perspectives: Objects examines the things that accompany humanitarian action — from standardized kits to improvised tools — revealing how design choices influence care, survival, and daily life. Spaces looks at the environments shaped by humanitarian interventions: camps, waiting areas, settlements, and infrastructures where people live through uncertainty, and where design can both support and constrain human experience. Imaginaries explores the images, technologies, and narratives through which crises are represented – and invites us to question how these representations shape our understanding of humanitarian action. This exhibition was developed in collaboration with the research project The Future of Humanitarian Design (HUD), which brings together researchers, designers, engineers, and humanitarian practitioners to explore how design and new technologies can contribute to improving humanitarian responses. OBJECTS From medical kits and prosthetics to tents, water containers, blankets, tools, and digital devices, humanitarian action relies on countless objects that accompany everyday life in situations of crisis. Circulating through humanitarian operations, these items are present in moments of emergency as well as recovery. They can support care and resilience, but they can also be associated with constraint, exclusion, or even violence, shaping how aid is delivered and how humanitarian interventions are experienced. Far from being neutral, these objects are designed. Their production involves networks of designers, engineers, humanitarian organisations, companies, donors, and the local actors who use them. Their form, materials, and contents reflect choices about whose needs are prioritised, who participates in their design, and how humanitarian responses are organised. Humanitarian objects therefore embody practical solutions but also dilemmas. Kits offer a clear example of this dynamic. Prepared in advance and ready for immediate use, they allow organisations to respond efficiently in difficult conditions. By assembling selected instruments, materials, and protocols, kits make humanitarian operations faster and more mobile while standardising how assistance is delivered. What is included determines what kinds of care can be provided; what is absent may remain beyond reach. At the same time, humanitarian objects rarely remain fixed. They evolve through experience in the field, technological innovation, and the improvisations of those who use them. People affected by crises often adapt or repurpose these objects — transforming tents into shops, containers into furniture, or tools into unexpected devices. These practices reveal forms of creativity and resilience that extend beyond the intentions of designers. This section brings together selected examples, including Red Cross kits from the Museum’s collections and beyond that are part of the installation focusing on kits as well as prostheses developed by EPFL-Essential Tech. text: Project ASSEMBLY : CLIMATE WEEK NEW YORK New York. September 22-25, 2026 Assembly is a scenography created for Swissnex during Climate Week NYC 2026 , the world’s largest climate event. Swissnex is the Swiss global network for education, research, and innovation, connecting Swiss and international communities through cultural and intellectual exchange. For three days, Swissnex brought together voices from the private sector, research, art and policy at Performance Space in New York’s East Village for collective thinking and dialogue around climate action. The result of a workshop with HEAD students, the scenography was conceived around scaffolding, one of the most recognizable elements of New York’s urban landscape. Few structures are as omnipresent, versatile, and paradoxical—at once temporary and permanent, protective and obstructive, invisible and iconic. Scaffolding was reimagined not only as a tool of construction but also as a framework for encounter and collective reflection, and was transformed into a stage for new forms of gathering, dialogue, and exchange. The design followed a zero-waste approach: the scaffolding structures assembled for the event were disassembled at the end, and all materials were returned to their source. The design drew on the morphology of the Swiss Alpine landscape, creating an immersive installation through structure, image and spatial experience. Scaffolding was transformed into three inhabitable structures symbolizing Swiss mountains, translating their topography into an architectural language of levels and elevations. Visitors were invited to use the lower levels for seating, while large LED screens above displayed moving images of the Swiss landscape, creating a living topography. head: Exhibition 13 HOUSES, 1 GARDEN – MAIA GRADUATE SHOW Geneva. June 5-12, 2026 ‘13 Houses, 1 Garden’ is a Masters diploma studio investigating alternative approaches to densification in the context of Ge
text: Exhibition 13 HOUSES, 1 GARDEN – MAIA GRADUATE SHOW Geneva. June 5-12, 2026 ‘13 Houses, 1 Garden’ is a Masters diploma studio investigating alternative approaches to densification in the context of Geneva. Taking place on a site in the vicinity of the HEAD – Genève Campus where mid-century houses are slated for demolition in favor of a large housing complex, interior architecture is used as an impulse for intentions and solutions against tabula rasa. Starting from the urban planning layout, the studio proposed to consider as a starting point an alternate future, where half of the houses are demolished to propose denser housing solutions, while keeping 13 houses in the middle of the plot. Surrounded by 3 new housing buildings, these houses and their gardens form a new common space for the inhabitants. Students experimented with transforming these buildings through new uses, housing, cultural, leisure, and outdoor programs, while rethinking the relationships between private and collective space. Building on individual themes explored in previous research, each student started working from the interior of one house. Each individual project is embedded in the same context and various ways of relating to it are possible and encouraged. One could propose to transform a house, or a part of it, or to insert an autonomous piece of design within it, or to add elements to a garden, etc. The outdoor environment is considered as an integral extension of interiors, elaborating on the disciplinary boundaries of interior architecture, and considering landscape as an inhabitable interior. The semester culminated in a cohesive group project, articulating individual intentions within a shared framework, adding a collective dimension to the project. The final collective exhibition highlights the complexities and contradiction of articulating a constellation of personal interventions into a feasible, coherent whole. text: Studio WELCOME CASINO Geneva. Spring 2026 The WELCOME CASINO studio explored the adaptive reuse of the Casino Campione d’Italia, designed by Mario Botta, into a refugee social integration center. Once the economic engine of Campione d’Italia, the monumental structure became, following the casino’s bankruptcy and closure in 2018, a symbol of mono-economic dependency and geopolitical exceptionality. Although the casino reopened in 2022 with a significantly reduced operation, the enormous scale of the thirteen-storey, 36,000-square-meter building remains disproportionate to both its current use and a town of fewer than 2,000 inhabitants. The studio took this condition of underuse as an opportunity to imagine how the building could accommodate new civic functions alongside its existing activities. The project was further informed by Campione’s exceptional territorial condition. An Italian exclave surrounded by Switzerland and Lake Lugano, Campione is a territory in which national, customs, fiscal, infrastructural, and everyday geographies do not fully coincide. Its largely invisible border contrasts sharply with the nearby Como–Chiasso corridor, which became a critical migration landscape during the European refugee crisis, where intensified Swiss border controls, readmissions, and restrictions on onward movement left hundreds of migrants stranded on the Italian side. Campione itself is not a migration hotspot, but its location within this wider border territory exposes a striking asymmetry: a boundary that remains almost imperceptible to residents, tourists, workers, and casino visitors can become a consequential apparatus of control for migrant bodies. Against this context, WELCOME CASINO proposed introducing a refugee integration and reception center into Botta’s monumental structure, generating a strong civic program for the town. The project examined how an architecture conceived around gambling, tourism, and economic extraction could be partially converted into an architecture of care, hospitality, and shared civic life. The juxtaposition also foregrounded radically different regimes of mobility within the same territory: those associated with leisure, labor, and capital, and those experienced by displaced people seeking protection and onward movement across European borders. Students were challenged to avoid producing a hermetic asylum object and instead conceive a porous civic infrastructure capable of enabling interaction between refugees and local inhabitants. The transformation sought to turn an introverted monument into an accessible and inclusive environment in which reception, accommodation, collective facilities, education, work, leisure, and public programs could coexist. Interventions were expected to achieve maximum effect with minimum means, privileging selective removal, on-site material reuse, temporary and adaptable systems, and creative reinterpretation rather than nostalgic imitation or total replacement. The studio ultimately examined how an oversized structure defined by mono-functionality could be reimagined as a plural and evolving public resource for both newcomers and residents. Rather than treating humanitarian architecture as an isolated response to emergency, WELCOME CASINO investigated how adaptive reuse might embed practices of reception and integration within existing civic and architectural structures. Through precise strategies of transformation, it asked whether humanitarian design could simultaneously address displacement, architectural obsolescence, and local fragility, producing dignified and specific spaces of hospitality while establishing new forms of shared civic life. text: Course CIRCULARITY AND MATERIALS Geneva, Spring 2026 How to understand and encourage the practice of reuse? This question was the main topic of the course Circularity and Materials. For this edition, the course took place at the La Fonte cultural center. The Halles de la Fonderie association and collective La Fonte proposed a temporary and enriching architectural repurposing of this building complex. The project did not propose a renovation of the Halles, recognizing that the neighborhood would change in a few years, but rather a deconstruction—not a demolition—to support urban development processes. The project consisted of two components: a cultural pole and a pole focused on the reuse of materials. The course aimed to provide an understanding of all reuse processes within a real-world project. In order to look at the different facets of it, three topics were explored during this 6-day course: THE FUTURE RESSOURCERIE A student team planned the implementation of a temporary resource center on site, by inventorying materials, proposing categorizations, and beginning the spatial planning of this space. THE PARTICIPATORY WORKSITE PROJECT During the course, students took part in the ongoing participatory worksite project together with the La Fonte Collectif and Galta Collectif. This way, they learned about reuse processes such as collecting material from the deconstruction site, transport operations, storage issues, adaptations, and reuse applications on the project site. Learning by doing allowed them to understand the reality of the process and the value of artisanal work. THE REUSE PROCESS In addition to the participatory worksite project and the development of the future ressourcerie, students also worked on the documentation of the project by conducting interviews, consulting archives, and observing. A documentation work was carried out in order to communicate and give value to the reuse process that had been implemented in this renovation project. This shared experience took the form of an open event, with the aim of sharing the work and valorizing and documenting the reuse process to encourage and facilitate this practice. head: Exhibition NO ONE SEES THEM LIKE WE DO, MILAN DESIGN WEEK 2026 Milan. April 20-26, 2026 Alcova, Milan Design Week As part of Milan Design Week 2026, HEAD – Genève presented No One Sees Them Like We Do
text: Exhibition NO ONE SEES THEM LIKE WE DO, MILAN DESIGN WEEK 2026 Milan. April 20-26, 2026 Alcova, Milan Design Week As part of Milan Design Week 2026, HEAD – Genève presented No One Sees Them Like We Do: Notes on Animal Interiors at Alcova, an exhibition imagined by the students of MAIA. Through six spatial narratives, the project explores the place of companion animals in our living spaces and opens up new perspectives on the relationship between humans and non-humans. THERE ARE SEVEN DOVES DANCING IN MY HOME, presented by Hugo Maia Schmitt, Letizia Milone Dancing Doves explores the relationship between humans and doves through sound, rhythm, and shared movement. The project revolves around a musical object placed within the space, activated by song, landings, and touch. Rather than training or controlling, the device creates a situation of co-presence where vibration becomes a shared ground. Through informal choreography and reciprocal listening, the project imagines a domestic interior shaped by the possibility of mutual complicity. DOGS ARE NOT ONLY CREATURES, presented by Stéphanie Hemidi, Kim Sherin Schönauer, Jérémy Troilo Wiggly Dogs explores the shared territory between humans and dogs through bodily movement and sensory perception. Conceived from a low, animal-centered point of view, the project transforms the domestic garden into a responsive landscape of objects, vegetation, cavities, and textures. Designed for running, sniffing, crawling, and play, the space fosters attunement between species. Drawing on a logic of becoming-with, the dog is considered not as a passive companion but as a co-actor of the environment. The outdoors becomes a site of encounter where shared exploration produces a situated, relational world. FROGS IN SEARCH OF WETLANDS, presented by Martino De Grandis, Ailyn Pieyre Hidden Frog questions contemporary forms of fascination, capture, and display of living beings. In contrast to the attraction for exotic species kept behind glass, the project shifts attention toward local amphibians and their threatened habitats. It proposes discreet, water-based infrastructures, places for cooling, hydration, and refuge, embedded within domestic and agricultural landscapes. Rather than spectacular observation, Hidden Frog advocates for a non-invasive ethic of care, where coexistence is shaped by attention to fragile environments, silent maintenance, and the awareness of absence. MEUW (Socius novus), presented by Jaemo Lee, Lisa Schober Meuw speculates on a world in which companionship is no longer embodied by a living animal, but by an artefact that mimics presence, attachment, and response. Neither pet nor machine, the object proposes an alternative form of relation—one that requires no care, no habitat, and no responsibility toward a living being. Carried, touched, and kept close, it reacts through surface, weight, and affect. The project questions whether intimacy can be simulated without domination, and whether replacing the animal might reveal both a desire for connection and an inability to sustain coexistence with the living. FEAST FOR RATS, presented by Matilde Arletti in collaboration with collective La Dalle (Angélique Kuenzle, Julie Chavaz) Feast for Rats overturns the usual hierarchies of domestic space by inviting the rat to the table. An omnipresent yet systematically rejected species, the rat becomes a legitimate guest, participating in an act of shared conviviality. Composed of bread, seeds, and edible matter, the table shifts from a site of consumption to a space of encounter, intimacy, and negotiation. By placing the rat at the center of a shared ritual, the project carried out by the collective LA DALLE (Julie Chavaz and Angélique Kuenzle) and the student Matilde Arletti questions boundaries of disgust, hospitality, and equality, proposing sharing as a first gesture of interspecies recognition. text: Studio NO ONE SEES THEM LIKE WE DO Geneva. Spring 2026 This project is part of an ongoing research focused on the material and spatial conditions of interspecies cohabitation. Through theoretical contributions and case studies, the symposium framed domestic space as a site of negotiation—between enclosure and openness, shared environments, sensory dispositifs, digital mediation, care, and constraint. These perspectives inform a pedagogical ap­pro­ach where design operates as a critical tool rather than a re­presenta­tio­nal one. The research opens toward a book project bringing together essays, archives, teaching experiments, and speculative narratives, proposing an expanded understanding of interior architecture that acknowledges animal agency and evolving forms of shared habitation. text: Studio THERMAL RENOVATION Geneva. Fall 2025 Building H on the HEAD campus, originally constructed in 1910 and renovated in 1944 by architect Jean Erb, is an industrial structure that once belonged to the Tavaro factory, known for producing sewing machines for the Swiss brand Elna. Characterized by a concrete load-bearing structure and concrete façade infill with large windows, the building lacks thermal insulation. This condition led to significant heat loss in winter, increased energy consumption, and thermal discomfort for users due to cold surfaces. In summer, rising temperatures and substantial solar gains through the large openings caused overheating and further discomfort. The studio unfolded in three phases. It began with an exploration of the modes of heat exchange—conduction, convection, evaporation, and radiation. Students then investigated the spatial qualities associated with these phenomena through a program-free exercise on a 6 m × 6 m × 6 m volume. In the final phase, the acquired technical and design knowledge was applied to a thermal renovation project for Building H. Throughout the semester, invited experts and dedicated lectures supported the students in developing a solid understanding of thermal comfort and energy-related challenges in contemporary architecture. text: Workshop BODIES WITHIN INTERIOR SPACES, TROUBLING DOMESTICITIES Geneva. Fall 2025 Geneva Bodies Within Spaces, Troubling Domesticities is a design-research course based on the observation that space plays an active role in maintaining power relations over and between bodies. It argues that our material environment is not a neutral backdrop that accommodates the everyday lives of pre-established identities, bodies, and social interactions, but rather actively participates in shaping them. By focusing on domestic territories, the class aims to unravel the contemporary biopolitics of the home as a spatial regime of control that contributes to the construction of the “normal” body. Through the critical reinterpretation of pre-narrated domesticities, it seeks to renegotiate power dynamics embedded in space by unsettling the morphologies through which domestic activities and limitations are materially articulated. The normal body has been the primary inhabitant of architectural discourse for centuries. From the proporzioni del corpo umano secondo Vitruvio (Vitruvius, 1490), depicting a young white athletic man, to Architects’ Data (Neufert, 1936), developed within a historical context shaped by nationalist and eugenic conceptions of the human body; to the Modulor (Le Corbusier, 1945), again modeled on a white athletic male figure; and Joe and Josephine (Dreyfuss, 1955), a standardized male body this time accompanied by his wife, these images have defined spaces, objects, and spatial dimensions around us by defining their embedded social, gender, racial, and class attributions. These figures have also participated in the construction of their mirror images, implicitly defining which bodies were deemed deviant and monstrous within their territorial and political contexts. Their models, together with other disciplinary tools, contributed to the crystallization of disabled bodies not only in terms of mobility, but also along mental, gender, sexual, racial, and class lines. By focusing on domestic practices, this class proposes to examine the construction of the body through the shaping of intimacy and subjectivity. The contemporary Western home has been produced as a tightly delimited spatial property, organized through hierarchical, functional, and typological units, drawing upon the social diagram of the nuclear, heteronormative family. With the emergence of neoliberal work regimes and the corresponding dissolution of stable space-time boundaries, domesticities have undergone profound mutations. Professional practices now spill into the confines of the home, transforming its biopolitical structures and challenging the assumption of domestic space as fixed or self-contained. At the same time, as capitalist economic structures have increasingly privatized and individualized multiple forms of care work, particularly with the advent of home appliances, care workers have become both isolated and invisible. Paradoxically, this dissolution of the boundaries of domestic territories pressures bodies both inside and outside the home, while it may also offer the opportunity to question the privatization of domestic practices and to envision new possibilities for interdependent care beyond the household. By exploring domestic practices within the public sphere, we address these matters as public ones. Using fiction as a project methodology, Bodies Within Interior Spaces, Troubling Domesticities examines these mutations by observing and exploring spatial narratives of domesticity through which the modern notion of normalcy is articulated and imposed upon bodies. The course approaches care work as a critical lens through which the architectural discipline’s broader assumptions about bodies, productivity, autonomy, and dependency can be questioned. text: Workshop ANIMALS WITHIN INTERIOR SPACES Geneva. Fall 2025 Geneva This workshop demonstrated how interior architecture actively shapes modes of cohabitation between humans and animals, revealing domestication as a spatial, material, and cultural process rather than a purely biological one. Through collective research and speculative projects, students challenged the conventional notion of the “pet,” instead examining animals as ecological agents, symbolic figures, laborers, commodities, and co-inhabitants of domestic and urban environments. By engaging cases ranging from rats, pigeons, bees, snakes, fish, to selectively bred cats, the work exposed the ambivalence of domestication: animals are simultaneously integrated, exploited, aestheticized, and rendered dependent. Students showed how interiors—from aquariums and staircases to rooftops and furniture—mediate power relations, ethical responsibility, and sensory experience, often transforming animals’ behaviors, bodies, and lifeworlds. The outcomes highlight interior design as a critical tool for rethinking coexistence, capable of either reinforcing domination or enabling more attentive, reciprocal forms of inhabitation across species. text: Workshop PLANTS WITHIN INTERIOR SPACES Geneva. Fall 2025 A commodity, a marker of colonial power, a sign of wealth or status, a soft counterpoint to the germophobic modernist home. A commercial strategy to attract consumers, a metaphor for a broken relationship with our surroundings, a symbol of a domesticated planet, or of a lost Eden. An emblem of domesticity and care for the household, a representation of a forgotten – or imagined – relationship with the non-human world. An approximation of the garden one can’t afford to own, or would have no time to maintain. Over the past five thousand years, indoor plants have covered a spectrum of roles and conveyed a contradictory variety of meanings. Within commercial or sacred spaces, from medicinal to decorative selections, cared for like important guests from a faraway land, or left in a corner, dusty and in need of attention, hosted in temples and corporate lobbies, in extravagant conservatories and tiny flats, plants have been our flatmates. This workshop focused on the design of spaces that foreground the relationships between humans, plants, and the built environment. Student projects explored how plants embody ecological, cultural, historical, and symbolic significance, transforming interiors into sites of interaction, reflection, and care. Some interventions highlighted the sensuality and ethics of plant life, such as pollination and circadian rhythms, while others addressed plants historically considered invasive or marginalized, like nettles and mandrakes, turning fear or exclusion into curiosity and presence. Several projects integrated ecological processes, including phytopurification, to reveal cycles of matter, water, and life, making invisible natural systems legible within domestic or architectural spaces. By combining myth, science, and design, the works examined temporality, resilience, and the paradoxical roles of plants, creating environments where humans and non-human life coexist, communicate, and shape one another, emphasizing plants as agents of transformation, symbolism, and ecological reflection. text: Workshop CARE FOR YOUR HEAD ! Geneva. September 2025 The workshop Care for your HEAD! invited participants to closely observe the campus and ask a simple question: How can design improve life here? Over the course of a week, participants analyzed the spaces, uses, and daily life at HEAD in order to imagine and carry out concrete, full-scale (1:1) interventions—furniture, installations, micro-architectures… These interventions were modest or playful, yet functional—gestures that cared for everyone and helped transform the school into a more comfortable, welcoming, and lively place. Beyond the act of designing, the workshop was an invitation to experiment, build, test, and adapt—to reflect on how design shapes the way we live, meet, and share. text: Architecture ARCHITECTURE & MEDIA – MAIA GRADUATE SHOW Spring 2025 The split between physical and digital spaces is obsolete, as they are now intricately intertwined, influencing and impacting each other seamlessly. Our social lives occur across media, in transmedia spaces whose design and regulation nobody takes responsibility for. As we gather through multiple layers of media we merge environments and create possibilities for meaningful exchange between people globally as well as further opportunities for manipulation, inequality, and concentration of power. The internet enabled social interaction in and around previously disconnected physical spaces and digital assets, turning the formatting of information into the shaping of unprecedented transmedia realms. As architects we have a plural understanding of the public realm that is at once experiential, practical, and legislative. How do we contribute to the shaping of emerging transmedia worlds in ways that align with values of openness, inclusivity, sustainability, and fairness? The “MAIA Graduate Show 2025” invited visitors to explore how Interior Architecture can respond to shifting social, political, ecological, and technological conditions through imaginative and critical design. This year’s projects examined the intersections of care, visibility, intimacy, ritual, protest, and cohabitation, challenging traditional architectural norms and proposing alternative ways of inhabiting space through a diverse range of projects in terms of scale, typology, location, and complexity. Spanning through various themes and formats, the projects reimagined domestic environments, public infrastructure, sacred spaces, and urban voids. They transformed table linens into tools for social connection, explored the architectural imaginary shaped by media, cinema and tourism, examined protest architectures highlighting the imaginative breadth and critical urgency of the cohort’s work, used digital analysis to address the disappearance of glaciers, reimagined the spatial politics of high-income housing in New Delhi, investigated the auditory dimension of domestic life through a case study in Geneva’s social housing, reclaimed an abandoned urban site to create an intergenerational park where play becomes an inclusive activity and reimagined one of Hong Kong’s busiest public toilets as a civic space that centers care, dignity, and visibility. head: Course DE / CONSTRUCTION – STORIES OF APPLIED REUSE Spring 2025 How can we push the reuse of architectural structures and their materials? This question lies at the heart of an ongoing transformation
text: Course DE / CONSTRUCTION – STORIES OF APPLIED REUSE Spring 2025 How can we push the reuse of architectural structures and their materials? This question lies at the heart of an ongoing transformation at Route de Meyrin 49 in Geneva — an office building from the 1980s, originally constructed for Swisscom, now in the process of being reimagined as residential housing. The ambition of the project: to reuse the existing materials and structural elements wherever possible, promoting and testing the potential of circularity in architecture at scale. For six days, MAIA students from HEAD engaged directly with this question, not through theory but through physical, labour-intensive action. We were given access to the first floor of the building —a raw site where we could dismantle, intervene, and experiment. It became a space of learning and unlearning, of listening to the building through its materials. The process began with cataloguing and categorising the elements we encountered from walls to surrounding plantations. The act of reuse requires deep attention. It is a slow choreography of subtraction and addition: dismantling what was, so something else can take form. Each act is deliberate, and each gesture matters. Ceilings were removed, walls opened, cavities revealed. A building, raw, layered, and full of stories. Taking it apart is not destruction; it’s a form of reading. text: Studio TEMPORARY TECTURE Spring 2025 The TEMPORARY TECTURE studio explored the design of temporary modular buildings, emphasizing the concept of “design for disassembly” in architecture. By incorporating time as a crucial factor in construction, the studio aligned with circular economy principles, considering the future use of building elements as an integral part of the design process. It investigated how urgent spatial challenges could be addressed with quick, temporary solutions without compromising aesthetics, quality, climate comfort, or ecological performance. The studio began with research into various temporary building typologies, such as container housing for refugees, shelters for construction workers, modular schools, hospitals, and kindergartens, as well as other provisional structures. It was grounded in the principles of anonymous infrastructural architecture, as outlined in the book Con Temporary Archi Tecture by KOSMOS architects. Students were challenged to design temporary and provisional buildings that responded to contemporary social, urban, and political issues. These structures prioritized rapid, industrialized construction, minimal site impact (no excavation or permanent foundations), and future disassembly, making them both resilient and environmentally responsible. The history of modular and prefabricated architecture was marked by cycles of innovation and decline. This studio critically examined how these familiar technologies could be reimagined to produce humane, ecological buildings with responsible material use, innovative aesthetics, and a strong focus on novel interior design. head: Studio LIVING IN GENEVA IN 2100 Geneva, Fall 2024 Global warming in Europe, with its effects in terms of heatwaves, droughts, floods, and their damaging consequences for life, is already being felt. I
text: Studio LIVING IN GENEVA IN 2100 Geneva, Fall 2024 Global warming in Europe, with its effects in terms of heatwaves, droughts, floods, and their damaging consequences for life, is already being felt. It is projected to increase by another 4°C by 2100. The climate in Geneva at that time is not expected to resemble the current climate; instead, it will likely resemble that of Hamburg. Geneva itself is projected to experience a climate similar to that of Mexico, Japan, North Africa, or Sicily. The studio LIVING IN GENEVA IN 2100 proposes acquiring practical knowledge of interior design tools to combat global warming by ensuring sustainable thermal living conditions in the face of summer heatwaves and winter cold. If the city is to remain livable, if living things are to survive, and if human beings are to continue living in Geneva in 2100, architecture and the city must already be conceived, adapted, and built with a climate similar to the one currently existing further south. Our project for MAIA, therefore, aims to study interior architecture and decoration suited to warmer Mediterranean, Central American, and Asian climates, and to imagine, propose, and test their immediate acclimatization for Swiss cities and culture, ensuring that life for humans, plants, and animals can still be possible in 2100. The semester was divided into different phases, alternating between research and design. The program focused on living in Geneva and culminated in the creation of prototype decorative elements. head: Studio PERMEABLE SPECIES (NOUS AVONS FAILLI COMMENCER SANS VOUS) Geneva, Fall 2024 Permeable Species is part of a larger research series that BUREAU (Daniel Zamarbide, Carine Pimenta, Galliane Zamarbi
text: Studio PERMEABLE SPECIES (NOUS AVONS FAILLI COMMENCER SANS VOUS) Geneva, Fall 2024 Permeable Species is part of a larger research series that BUREAU (Daniel Zamarbide, Carine Pimenta, Galliane Zamarbide) will develop over the coming years, which began at the Laval School of Architecture in Canada in 2023. Under the title Nous Avons Failli Commencer Sans Vous (We Almost Started Without You), this research aims to study the spatial conditions that might allow us to rethink, revisit, and upgrade our relationships with other species. We explore possibilities for cohabitation and experiment with unconventional methods and tools to produce architectural and design pieces. At MAIA, the Permeable Species studio focused on designing co-habitational spaces where we include ourselves—humans, bodies, and permeable beings—within the multiple and constitutive relationships that form us and that we are part of. The studio achieved this by fostering companionship and neighborly relations with other species. Every student partnered with a companion species and developed their own relationship with them, designing spaces to accommodate this interaction. We worked with two forms of research media: film and a manufactured object—one virtual, one physical. Both require craft and careful making. Both are intended as media to develop a story to be told and shown. Projects in the studio were viewed as stories, Speculative Fabulations (Donna Haraway) that addressed urgent realities. It is urgent that we think of ourselves differently—as multiple beings and as part of a different world balance, one that is more Gaian (Lovelock, Margulis). The spaces we inhabit—those we practice, perform, and activate—must be redefined in relation to the multiplicity of being. They must open up, be porous, and permeable. The conceptual framework of the studio was thus closely tied to a very tangible and material approach. Ideas existed only when they took material form. The studio was fundamentally conceived as a space for making—a workshop. Spontaneous intuition was prioritized to quickly explore how projects could materialize. In this sense, the speculative aspect of the studio was grounded in material, technical, and non-abstract pragmatism. Both students and the team understood well how things are made and what things are made of. Discover more about the project on the dedicated website Permeable Species and on e-flux . head: Thesis INTERIOR ECOLOGIES THESIS Geneva, Spring 2025 Developed as part of the Master of Arts in Interior Architecture (MAIA) program at HEAD – Genève, this series of MA theses expands the field of int
text: Thesis INTERIOR ECOLOGIES THESIS Geneva, Spring 2025 Developed as part of the Master of Arts in Interior Architecture (MAIA) program at HEAD – Genève, this series of MA theses expands the field of interior architecture through critical investigations into the socio-political, ecological, and sensory dimensions of space. Engaging with themes such as protest, postcolonial modernity, sensory experience, planetary habitation, and material symbolism, the works reflect a growing interest in interiors as dynamic, performative sites of negotiation and transformation. These theses articulate new relationships between bodies, objects, and environments—foregrounding questions of visibility, labor, ritual, and resistance. Corridors, thresholds, doors, and domestic atmospheres are re-examined not only as architectural elements but as spatial agents that mediate intimacy, identity, and collective belonging. Protest infrastructures, ceremonial practices, and ephemeral gastronomic events are explored as alternative typologies that challenge normative frameworks of use and function. Informed by interdisciplinary methodologies, these projects respond to contemporary conditions through a redefinition of spatial practices. They propose renewed modes of engagement that foreground memory, materiality, and multisensory experience, situating interior architecture as a critical and responsive discipline capable of navigating the complexities of both terrestrial and extraterrestrial ecologies. head: Future ARCHITECTURAL LATENT SPACE Geneva, Spring 2025 With the rise of generative artificial intelligence, parametric design, and immersive digital environments, architecture is no longer limited to t
text: Future ARCHITECTURAL LATENT SPACE Geneva, Spring 2025 With the rise of generative artificial intelligence, parametric design, and immersive digital environments, architecture is no longer limited to the built. It extends into media territories—speculative, latent, and conceptual. Contemporary tools are no longer used solely to represent projects, but to generate forms, narratives, and hypotheses that are not necessarily intended to exist physically. The image becomes the project. Architecture becomes a field of visual emergence. This course explores the critical potentials of this transformation. Through the activation of a latent space—a terrain of hybridization between styles, programs, narratives, and representational regimes—students were invited to create an Instagram account presenting a project positioned at the intersection of architectural speculation, visual storytelling, and tool critique. Each project presented here takes a unique stance. Far from seductive renderings or easy fictions, these works challenge norms: What power does style still hold? How is a spatial narrative constructed? What remains of the author when images precede intention? What regimes of truth and ambiguity must architecture now confront? In a world where the circulation of images is instantaneous, synthetic, and algorithmic, mastering these technologies is no longer just a technical act—it is a theoretical one. It is no longer simply about illustrating architecture, but about producing it as a critical field, a narrative space, and a performative fiction. head: Workshop PLANTS WITHIN INTERIOR SPACES Geneva, Fall 2024 A commodity, a marker of colonial power, a sign of wealth or status, a soft counterpoint to the germophobic modernist home. A commercial strate
text: Workshop PLANTS WITHIN INTERIOR SPACES Geneva, Fall 2024 A commodity, a marker of colonial power, a sign of wealth or status, a soft counterpoint to the germophobic modernist home. A commercial strategy to attract consumers, a metaphor for a broken relationship with our surroundings, a symbol of a domesticated planet, or of a lost Eden. An emblem of domesticity and care for the household, a representation of a forgotten – or imagined – relationship with the non-human world. An approximation of the garden one can’t afford to own, or would have no time to maintain. Over the past five thousand years, indoor plants have covered a spectrum of roles and conveyed a contradictory variety of meanings. Within commercial or sacred spaces, from medicinal to decorative selections, cared for like important guests from a faraway land, or left in a corner, dusty and in need of attention, hosted in temples and corporate lobbies, in extravagant conservatories and tiny flats, plants have been our flatmates. Today’s collections of moth orchids (Phalaenopsis), Swiss-cheese plants (Monstera deliciosa), or rubber figs (Ficus elastica) made their way to Western households a few centuries ago, as they left the care and taxonomical scope of botanical gardens and conservatories. They have since been selected through commerce for their capacity to thrive, or, at least, survive, in the harshest conditions – within polluted, dark, dry, or overheated rooms, subject to forgetful owners and irregular, man-made, mood-determined, weather patterns. Although absent in the grand histories of architecture, houseplants are, within the home, the living connection with our planet’s air and soil, with everything that changes, moves, and transforms beyond our walls. Our first buildings were made of their bodies, and even the most modest snake plant (Dracaena trifasciata), forgotten on a shelf, purchased for a few francs, connects us to the sun and the earth. Within a room, we share intimacy with plants as individuals: at night, asleep, we breathe their body, as the oxygen their metabolism produced enters our own. This studio was dedicated to the design of a room for people and plants. The student projects explored the dynamic relationship between plants, culture, and architecture by transforming everyday spaces to reflect the symbolic, historical, and ecological roles of plants. The interventions ranged from creating communal areas that foster connection, to critiquing capitalism by reinterpreting plants as symbols of value and exchange. Some projects explored the representation of plant species across ecological zones, while others celebrated the medicinal qualities of certain species or challenged negative perceptions. Through these interventions, students explored the impact of plants in both architectural and social contexts, as well as their potential to serve as symbols, sources of resilience, and agents of change. head: Workshop CLIMATIC VILLA Villa Romaine, Hyères, France, September 2024 HEAD – Genève & École Camondo Climatic Villa is a workshop that explores the complexities and contradictions between architectural
text: Workshop CLIMATIC VILLA Villa Romaine, Hyères, France, September 2024 HEAD – Genève & École Camondo Climatic Villa is a workshop that explores the complexities and contradictions between architectural heritage and the new challenges posed by the global climate crisis. It took place in the unique setting of the historical Villa Romaine, located in the southern French city of Hyères. Once a luxurious private residence dedicated to pleasure and hedonism, Villa Romaine is now a preserved historical monument. However, it is no longer in active use, its future is uncertain, its maintenance is costly and complex, and its heritage status makes it difficult to imagine how it can transform in the future. This context—both opulent and problematic—created the perfect opportunity for students to reflect on questions of future adaptability, transformation, and the possibility of flexible uses for the Villa in the face of pressing climatic, environmental, and social crises. The workshop was a collaboration between two schools: HEAD – Genève and École Camondo Méditerranée. Imagining probable dystopian scenarios that society may face in the near future—such as water scarcity, floods, extreme heat, and air pollution—students developed 1:1 scale projects to transform different spaces within the Villa. They strategically reimagined the villa’s main hall, terrace, staircase, maintenance room, garden, and swimming pool into new programmatic typologies, speculating on key questions: How can preserved monuments adapt to future drastic challenges? What tools can help heritage buildings adequately respond to climatic and environmental issues? What new radical habitation scenarios and typologies can heritage buildings catalyze? head: Exhibition 2084: A DIORAMA OF THE FUTURE Alcova / Milan Design Week, April 2024 2084: A Diorama of the Future is an architectural speculation on the challenges of the post-Anthropocene era. The scenar
text: Exhibition 2084: A DIORAMA OF THE FUTURE Alcova / Milan Design Week, April 2024 2084: A Diorama of the Future is an architectural speculation on the challenges of the post-Anthropocene era. The scenario deals with the reconstruction of a near future in which some cities are submerged, while others endure extreme conditions, direct consequences of the climate emergency. Amidst this turbulence, a diverse group of human and non-human explorers parachutes into 2084, facing the challenge of survival and reconstruction. Designed by MAIA students, the project transforms part of the historic annexes of Villa Bagatti Valsecchi into a dynamic and performative diorama, inviting visitors to reflect on contemporary environmental and societal dilemmas. While 19th-century dioramas always presented romanticized visions of exotic natures behind glass screens that detached visitors from their complexities, Diorama of the Future inserts visitors right at the center of damaged environments, calling for new ecosystemic actions. In this large climatic device, both students and visitors take on the role of inhabitants of a changing vivarium, whose evolution problematizes the relation between vision, appropriation, and climate change. The project was designed by MAIA students under the direction of Youri Kravtchenko, assisted by Cecile-Diama Samb, and presented at Alcova for the Milan Design Week 2024. text: Project EPIC PICNIC Geneva, September 2024 EPIC PICNIC was a project for the European Heritage Days, held in Geneva in September 2024. Celebrating the built heritage of the city, it transformed Hentsch Park into a large-scale neighborhood picnic. EPIC PICNIC was organized by MAIA students on the former football field of Charmilles, which is surrounded by historic industrial buildings. The project explored the intersections between the city, its history, heritage, architecture, and societal evolution. EPIC PICNIC was inclusive, welcoming a wide range of human and non-human visitors of all ages, origins, genders, abilities, and spheres of belonging. It exemplified cases of glocalization and the intersections between high and low culture, with inclusivity at its core, ensuring accessibility and resonance across diverse demographics. EPIC PICNIC layered the space with music, dancing, sports, picnicking, chess, pétanque, stargazing, and film screenings, creating a day where past and present converged. Much like the tango, where dancers navigate the same space while avoiding collisions, the blend of various activities and participants created both complexity and beauty. Built under the commission of City of Geneva and the Journées Européennes du Patrimoine. head: Course CARING ARCHITECTURES Geneva, Spring 2024 Caring Architectures questions how the structural invisibility of both reproductive labor activities and their related spaces perpetuates power relation
text: Course CARING ARCHITECTURES Geneva, Spring 2024 Caring Architectures questions how the structural invisibility of both reproductive labor activities and their related spaces perpetuates power relations in the domestic realm. The course investigates domestic care spaces as reflections of the devaluation of care tasks through architectural theory. Modern Western housing continues the trend of optimizing and individualizing care spaces, a trend rooted in the late 19th century. While examining this patriarchal and capitalist legacy, the course also views these spaces as stages for daily practices, providing a form of bottom-up architectural knowledge. Fiction serves as a lens to understand power and resistance in spaces like laundry rooms, kitchens, closets, and garbage rooms, revealing their unremarkable power structures. Integrating interior architecture theory with feminist and queer literature, the course examines the material conditions of essential care in our built environment. It identifies the repetitive, daily performance of these spaces (Bonnevier, 2007), focusing on body politics and the interaction between interior architecture and working bodies. Housing production is approached as major architecture, with minor architectures rising within it (Stoner, 2012). These minor architectures maintain domesticities and highlight architecture’s socio-political responsibility concerning care, repair, and decay (Malterre-Barthes, 2019). Over six days, each module focuses on one care task and its related spaces: cooking, cleaning, storing, ironing, shopping, sorting, etc. Shaped as design research, the work articulates the analysis of the pre-existing experience of one character, one selected fiction (from a film or a novel), the space that stages the fiction, and texts from both architectural theory and queer/feminist literature. The course uses and develops diverse tools, from architectural plans and models to readings and writings, in order to foster collective discussion, problematize, and rewrite spatial narratives of care. head: Future ARCHITECTURAL HACK: AI-generated architecture offices Geneva, Spring 2024 With the advancement of digital technologies, especially generative AI, big data analysis, and deep fakes, interior arc
text: Future ARCHITECTURAL HACK: AI-generated architecture offices Geneva, Spring 2024 With the advancement of digital technologies, especially generative AI, big data analysis, and deep fakes, interior architecture has shifted from construction to media. This shift has created a new digital ecology that blurs the lines between what is considered real—the physical—and what has historically been considered fake—the virtual. This project aims to explore these entanglements by utilizing generative AI to expedite design processes. The challenge is to establish fictional yet believable architecture offices that gain recognition within a few days by exclusively using AI-generated content. To achieve this, MAIA students need to: conceive a storyline for the office, design a website presenting the office and its projects, create profiles of fictitious architects with resumes and professional backgrounds, design simulated built projects to enrich the agency’s portfolio, develop a social media presence on different platforms, and publish fabricated press articles that discuss the office, thereby increasing its visibility and credibility. Three AI-generated architecture offices were created in one week: Schröder/Schröder øona collective Anarchy Spatial Structures Methodologically, Architectural Hack explores the transformation of the architectural profession, which has always required teamwork, a structured environment, and technological mediation. Recently, public AI services (ChatGPT, Midjourney, etc.) have enabled the handling of tasks previously assigned to humans and promise to accelerate the production time of design projects. Similarly, skills such as using document-sharing services (cloud, intranet, etc.) and organizing internal files have become crucial to ensuring effective work. More broadly, the project illustrates how autonomy in finding information through tutorials and web resources is entangled with collective design processes in AI-mediated environments. text: Studio EDELWEISS HOUSE Geneva, Fall 2023 Edelweiss House explores the construction of a new greenhouse solution in Geneva, not in the style of the 19th-century building type, where Western societies sought to replicate the warmth of milder climates through fossil fuels. Instead, we propose a climatically inverted approach—a cold greenhouse befitting the 21st century. Here, the societies of a West that has become too warm aim to emulate the coolness of milder climates, perhaps reminiscent of times past, thanks to renewable energies. In contrast to the 19th-century “Palm House,” we propose designing an “Edelweiss House”—a structure creating a cold microclimate within the currently scorching macro-climate of the West. The intention of the studio is to provide students with both the theoretical and practical means to respond to the transformations of climates resulting from global warming in terms of habitability while striving to reduce greenhouse gas emissions to limit ongoing global warming. After a few weeks of research, students analyzed and applied practical architectural solutions to survive in increasingly hot temperatures while implementing low-carbon strategies to reduce the energy consumed in building operation and through the type of materials and construction to limit CO2 emissions. This initial climatic approach to architecture was combined with an ecological approach through an understanding of the physiology of living beings and plants in terms of chemical, physical, and biological exchanges, light, humidity, temperature, and nutrition required for survival. The semester was organized around a balance between research and design, enabling architectural solutions to be based on a solid understanding of the climatic, chemical, physical, and biological phenomena involved. The proposed pavilion, a new contemporary Edelweiss House for the 21st century, was collectively built by the students at the end of the semester. head: Studio CINEMA IS A VERB : A Wall, a Tower and a Tent Geneva, Fall 2023 Cinema is a Verb is a Master’s studio that explores the intersection between a mode of construction (the temporary) and a very sp
text: Studio CINEMA IS A VERB : A Wall, a Tower and a Tent Geneva, Fall 2023 Cinema is a Verb is a Master’s studio that explores the intersection between a mode of construction (the temporary) and a very specific program (the movie theater). The cinema department at HEAD – Genève urgently requires a dedicated space for educational and event-based film screenings. After several phases of research, two proposals were developed in detail until the end of the semester. These two projects aim to reconcile the practical requirements of the program with the diverse imaginaries it encompasses. Project 1: A Wall, a Tower and a Tent A wall serves as a screen, and a projection tower creates two monoliths that fictively have been there forever, shaping the space and giving form to the tent. A square within a circle follows the plan dictated by primitive shapes. A metal structure forms the skeleton, standing independently on the school’s terrace. Layers of fabric cover the whole. An umbrella, a coat, and underwear dresses protect the structure and the visitors from the elements. Closed for watching a film, open for hosting festivities. The building, delicately placed on top of the school, inevitably evokes the collective imagination of the circus and a form of festive lightness reminiscent of the first film screenings. head: Workshop CIRCULARITY AND MATERIALS Geneva, November 2023 How can we see value and potential in resources that are destined to be thrown away? How can they be valorized and put back into circulation? T
text: Workshop CIRCULARITY AND MATERIALS Geneva, November 2023 How can we see value and potential in resources that are destined to be thrown away? How can they be valorized and put back into circulation? This year, the Circularity course took place in a disused industrial area in the north of Geneva. Occupied until recently, the buildings were due to be demolished. A restaurant, a fitness center, a garage, and a warehouse served as a case study for the students during six days. In groups of two, students were assigned to different categories: floors, walls, ceilings, lighting, carpentry, HVAC, and fixed furniture. They first carried out a diagnosis of the resources present on-site to identify the building’s components, understand their composition and dimensions, and analyze how they were installed. A collection of inventory sheets emerged. Following the identification of these resources, they were able to experiment with a careful dismantling of the components. This also enabled them to confirm or deny their potential and the possibility of dismantling. A “ressourcerie,” shared by the whole class and representative of the different categories, was set up directly on-site. Portraying the resources out of their initial context made it easier to appropriate them and conceive a future use. The dismantled components were then used to develop various proposals with the aim of upcycling and putting them back into circulation. Therefore, each group targeted potential actors and addressed them with two formal proposals. On one hand, a proposition with the same initial use, such as restoring parquet floors, staircases, or lighting fixtures; on the other, a proposition that illustrated the diversity of potential uses, such as the creation of exhibition podiums using false ceiling panels, the construction of a deckchair from sauna wood, or the development of a table’s collection with various legs and plates. A final exhibition was set up directly on-site to present the work carried out to a number of actors in Geneva’s construction and re-use field. At the same time, documentation work was carried out throughout the course to illustrate the various stages and highlight the value of the work process. head: Exhibition APPROPRIATE BARRAGÁN 29.09.2023 - 07.04.2024, Barragán Gallery, Vitra Schaudepot, Weil-am-Rhein Photograph exhibition from the workshop Appropriate Barragán, led by Bas Princen As part of a
text: Exhibition APPROPRIATE BARRAGÁN 29.09.2023 - 07.04.2024, Barragán Gallery, Vitra Schaudepot, Weil-am-Rhein Photograph exhibition from the workshop Appropriate Barragán, led by Bas Princen As part of a partnership formed in 2022 between the Vitra Design Museum and the Barragan Foundation, the archive of Mexican architect Luis Barragán (1902-1988) was transferred to new premises at the Vitra Schaudepot. This move was accompanied by the creation of the Barragán Gallery, a public exhibition space that offers insights into the architect’s life and work. From September 29, 2023, to April 7, 2024, a new presentation at the gallery showcases photographs made by students from the Geneva University of Art and Design (HEAD – Genève) and the CENTRO School of Design, Film, and Digital Media in Mexico City. The images were produced as part of the joint workshop Appropriate Barragán, led by photographer Bas Princen. Luis Barragán’s architecture has gained wide renown, due in no small part to the circulation of a limited number of carefully selected photographs. These photographs, realized by Armando Salas Portugal in close collaboration with the architect, have created a particular perception of Barragán’s work. They attach a distinctive aura to Barragán’s spaces and contribute to their iconic status by emphasizing characteristics such as light, color, and form. One could even postulate that Barragán designed spaces with the eyes of his photographer in mind. The workshop Appropriate Barragán, led by Bas Princen in the summer of 2022, brought together design students from HEAD – Genève and CENTRO Mexico City in a joint project to experience, analyze, and interpret major architectural works by Luis Barragán through the medium of photography. They captured some unexpected views of two well-known buildings, the Barragán House and the Prieto López House (also known as Casa Pedregal), producing distinctive visual impressions of intimacy, space, lighting, architectural details, and traces of habitation. Research for the trip commenced with a visit to the Barragán Gallery in Weil am Rhein, along with an introduction to the architect’s collection of photographs, which is preserved in the Barragán Archive. At the conclusion of the workshop in Mexico City, the students collectively created a unified presentation of their studies, with each student proposing a selection of images to be displayed in specific dimensions. This setting is replicated in the exhibition of the respective works in the Barragán Gallery. This exhibition is part of the initiative to open the Barragán Archive for research and collaborations, which will be continued in the coming years. head: Workshop DOMESTICITY / DOMESTICATION: THE ANIMAL AT HOME Geneva, November 2023 Instead of situating interior architecture as an all-encompassing field that designs the domestic cohabitation of animals
text: Workshop DOMESTICITY / DOMESTICATION: THE ANIMAL AT HOME Geneva, November 2023 Instead of situating interior architecture as an all-encompassing field that designs the domestic cohabitation of animals and humans, this workshop uses this discipline to critically examine the validity of this historical phenomenon from a material and spatial perspective. Moving away from the notion of a “pet” – questioned by new theoretical approaches to the relationship between humans and non-humans – the workshop aims to identify the traditional role that interior design plays in animal domestication within home interiors. Its ultimate goal is to envision non-hierarchical relations that diverge from the imposition of human-centric materials and spatial domestic standards onto other species. Students collectively work as a research unit on a graphic publication to be presented at the end of the workshop. After reading several key texts from fields such as the history of science, biology, and philosophy, they map out current discussions regarding the presence of animals in domestic spaces through clippings from general printed and online media written in the languages each student speaks. This includes new legal frameworks, political polemics, the transformation of the home, the design of new architectural artifacts, etc. As a means of making the workshop’s discussions public, students’ ongoing research is presented through MAIA’s online platforms. head: Workshop UFO (Unidentified Floating Objects) Geneva, September 2023 HEAD – Genève & École Camondo The Unidentified Floating Objects (UFOs) project unfolded as a captivating exploration into the intric
text: Workshop UFO (Unidentified Floating Objects) Geneva, September 2023 HEAD – Genève & École Camondo The Unidentified Floating Objects (UFOs) project unfolded as a captivating exploration into the intricacies of Lake Léman’s inhabited waters and the dynamic interplay between humans and the mid-water ecosystem. Over the course of a five-day workshop, groups of students embarked on a creative journey, conceptualizing and fabricating floating devices designed to serve diverse programmatic purposes. The culmination of their efforts materialized on the final day, as participants collectively ventured onto the serene expanse of Lake Léman, navigating the waters within the confines of their ingeniously crafted architectures. Lake Léman and the adjacent Rhône River served as the canvas for a plethora of floating structures, each uniquely engineered to fulfill distinct functions. Among these innovative constructs were devices dedicated to filtering and purifying the water, delving beneath its surface to meticulously measure its properties, inhabiting the water’s upper layers, effortlessly traversing through its depths, and seamlessly transitioning between different bodies of water and organisms for interactive engagement. The exploration of these activities provided valuable insights into the contemporary relationship shared between water resources and the daily life of the Geneva populace. A noteworthy aspect of the project lay in its commitment to sustainability, as all architectural devices were constructed using solely reused materials. This eco-conscious approach not only underscored the students’ creativity and resourcefulness but also reflected a conscientious effort to minimize environmental impact. As a manifesto of the ethos of the workshop, once the exploration phase concluded, all structures were meticulously dismantled and carefully stored for future reuse, embodying a commitment to responsible and mindful design practices. The Unidentified Floating Objects initiative succeeded not only in fostering a deeper understanding of the delicate balance within Lake Léman’s ecosystem but also in showcasing the potential for innovative, sustainable solutions in the realm of aquatic architecture. The collaborative efforts of the students, coupled with their commitment to ecological responsibility, left an intangible mark on the shores of Lake Léman, serving as an inspiring example for future endeavors at the intersection of human activity and environmental stewardship. head: Exhibition INTERIOR ECOLOGIES – MAIA GRADUATE SHOW Geneva, Spring 2023 INTERIOR ECOLOGIES is an ongoing project by MAIA, the Master of Arts in Interior Architecture at HEAD – Genève. It investigates a
text: Exhibition INTERIOR ECOLOGIES – MAIA GRADUATE SHOW Geneva, Spring 2023 INTERIOR ECOLOGIES is an ongoing project by MAIA, the Master of Arts in Interior Architecture at HEAD – Genève. It investigates architecture at the intersection of space and ecology, questioning the default association of this field with territorial scales, and claiming that interior spaces construct multiscalar ecologies from within. Space design is seen as multidimensional, articulating the diversity of interiors, environments, and multispecies that configure reality across many paths and scales, from material to virtual, and from local to global. The “MAIA Graduate Show 2023” invited visitors to delve into the intricate interplay between the natural, artificial, and digital realms within the contemporary built environment. The exhibition explored how ecology is shaping the discipline of Interior Architecture in the 21st century. The interpretation of this theme was intentionally left open for students, resulting in projects that address environmentally responsible construction, ecology, reuse, energy efficiency, social and political urgencies, as well as novel materials and technologies. Visitors had the opportunity to witness a diverse range of projects in terms of scale, typology, location, and complexity. These included a refugee shelter crafted from mushrooms, a communal neighborhood kitchen in Geneva, the transformation of a water tank into housing in India, the creation of a new social center facilitating the exchange of reused materials, a furniture collection derived from repurposed office carpets, and numerous other projects that express the pressing need for a transformative paradigm in architectural production. Ultimately, INTERIOR ECOLOGIES explores both the responses to contemporary environmental and societal challenges (carbon footprint, circular economy, etc.) and the implications of new ecological paradigms (post-human, more-than-human, etc.) for interior architecture as a discipline in all its professional dimensions—space design, product design, new media, research, curatorial, and editorial practices. head: Studio HOW TO ENVISION THE FUTURE OF LIVING AND WORKING IN TIMES OF ECOLOGICAL CRISIS? Geneva, Spring 2023 During the spring semester of 2023, seven students of the Master in Interior Architecture (MA
text: Studio HOW TO ENVISION THE FUTURE OF LIVING AND WORKING IN TIMES OF ECOLOGICAL CRISIS? Geneva, Spring 2023 During the spring semester of 2023, seven students of the Master in Interior Architecture (MAIA) at HEAD – Genève developed their own studio space through prospective scenarios on living and working in 2050. It had been a while since the group noticed certain changes in their surrounding world. Everything approached discreetly, making it hard to distinguish one day from the next. As they attempted to navigate the world as usual, they quickly realized it was not the same. Thus, they faced an exceptional level of consumption, which eventually led to ecological disaster on one hand and emotional exhaustion on the other. Choosing between the catastrophe of the mundane, they disagreed on which was worse. The only shared point of view appeared to be a firm belief that something should be done. Finding their soulmates, each squad chose its own way to cope with the modern world. What happened next? By revisiting daily rituals that construct reality, they focused on its initial qualities and the transformations that took place. Excited to find a cure, they explored casual activities like sleeping, mealtime, and gathering together. Each squad aspired to find solutions for daily issues. Some chose to address it through close interaction, while others chose alienation. Did they succeed? text: Thesis INTERIOR ECOLOGIES THESIS Geneva, Spring 2023 Developed as part of the Master of Arts in Interior Architecture (MAIA) program at HEAD – Genève, this series of MA theses explores the theme of interior ecologies, investigating the interconnections between interior spaces, environments, and media through successive decentralizations: from the historical human-built totalitarianism that has existed for centuries (inclusivity) to the relationship with non-humans (ecology), and finally, the connection to machines and virtual environments (technology). The theses advocate for a vision in which the human and the non-human are articulated in new parliamentary assemblies, mastering the professional aspects of the project and studying the public, private, and commercial spheres of contemporary interiors. head: Workshop CIRCULARITY Geneva, December 2022 Nowadays, construction stands out as one of the most polluting sectors. What was once perceived as a source of value a few centuries ago has transformed into
text: Workshop CIRCULARITY Geneva, December 2022 Nowadays, construction stands out as one of the most polluting sectors. What was once perceived as a source of value a few centuries ago has transformed into a wellspring of waste. We grapple with the overconsumption of materials, equipment, and lighting, to the detriment of the environment and people’s well-being. As interior architects, we find ourselves compelled to transform, renew, and rearrange various spaces to meet the evolving demands, usage, and identity renewal of a place. However, the “usual” processes often entail replacing a substantial amount of still viable materials with new raw materials. How can we prioritize the use of local resources? In the context of an in-situ workshop within a building destined for renovation, Master of Arts students in Interior Architecture from HEAD – Genève delved into the potential reuse of materials on-site. This workshop complemented theoretical and practical courses covering the themes of reuse, deconstruction, and eco-conception. How has reuse evolved throughout the history of architecture? How can we implement reuse in today’s context? What processes should be in place to achieve this, and who are the key actors involved? What if we learned to deconstruct a building to better understand how to design the next one? The students initiated the course by developing a method to inventory the material components of the building. Doors, false ceilings, metal structures, and other building components were dismantled by the students to understand the deconstruction processes and assess their possibilities for reuse. All these resources were then consolidated in one room – an ephemeral warehouse of reusable materials – from which the students were free to draw inspiration to develop their own projects. Taking the materials out of their original context helped rediscover these resources from a different perspective. This approach required a rethinking of design processes, utilizing available materials as inspiration for project development rather than starting from a drawing. The exhibition showcases the materials in their original context, dismantled, and repurposed as pieces of furniture. Consequently, each item of furniture has its own history and is showcased to highlight the potential of materials that were initially destined for waste. The collection includes assembly instructions, indicating how to reproduce the items and the required amount of material. head: Studio SHOULD THE PENCIL BE CREDITED AS THE AUTHOR TOO? HOW THE NON-HUMAN IS DRIVING INTERIOR ARCHITECTURE Geneva, Fall 2022-23 The abundance of energy provided by coal and oil for more than a century
text: Studio SHOULD THE PENCIL BE CREDITED AS THE AUTHOR TOO? HOW THE NON-HUMAN IS DRIVING INTERIOR ARCHITECTURE Geneva, Fall 2022-23 The abundance of energy provided by coal and oil for more than a century has gradually led us to lose our understanding of the natural dependence of human products and their aesthetics and design on material, non-human conditions, which actually participate as much in the success of artistic creation as human genius. What would 1960s aesthetics have looked like without oil, which made plastic and all the molded forms typical of the 1960s possible? What would the new millennium’s aesthetics look like without 3D software? What would modern aesthetics be without coal that made central heating and air conditioning possible? What would Roman architecture have looked like if Vitruvius had worked with AutoCAD? What shape would Le Corbusier’s buildings be if he had worked in 3D on Rhino? What would gothic cathedrals look like if universal gravity did not exist? What would Swiss chalets look like if there had been no snow? This interior design studio questioned the dependence of design on non-human material conditions of representation and construction, taking into account that not only pencils, erasers, ink, 2D software, 3D software, but also wood, earth, stone, rain, wind, and gravity can all be considered co-authors of the human project. head: Studio HOW DO WE BUILD TOGETHER? Geneva, Fall 2022-2023 The city of Geneva has a high office vacancy rate. This is due as much to the obsolescence of the offices as to the relocation of polluting acti
text: Studio HOW DO WE BUILD TOGETHER? Geneva, Fall 2022-2023 The city of Geneva has a high office vacancy rate. This is due as much to the obsolescence of the offices as to the relocation of polluting activities from the secondary sector towards peri-urban or even international areas. This high rate of vacancy contrasts with local needs for temporary housing, and more particularly student housing. For this project, we worked in collaboration with La Ciguë Genève, whose mandate was to repurpose vacant office buildings into student housing. While for the past 20 years, the city’s urban development doctrine has favored demolition for rebuilding with increased density, a shortage of resources and a growing awareness of ordinary heritage compel us to rethink and take a different approach. In our case, the aim has been to preserve rather than destroy, and to reuse rather than consume. The singular feature of this studio was that students occupied and modified their object of enquiry—an empty building awaiting demolition at Rue des Maraîchers 5, Geneva—throughout the semester. The students thus gradually appropriated the building to work and live. Inhabiting this space enabled them to conduct in-depth observations, taking into account dimensions relating to inhabitancy. While the building at Maraîchers 5 turned into a place of life and work with numerous challenges, it has also, and most importantly, fostered new connections, friendships, and ideas between students, urban actors, and local residents. head: Symposium INTERIOR ECOLOGIES Geneva, December 2022 HEAD – Genève, Geneva The conference aimed to bring together a series of transversal personalities who addressed the subject of non-human architectur
text: Symposium INTERIOR ECOLOGIES Geneva, December 2022 HEAD – Genève, Geneva The conference aimed to bring together a series of transversal personalities who addressed the subject of non-human architecture. From simple greenhouses to botanic facilities, data centres and automated interiors, never before in history has architecture produced so many interiors for the non-human, challenging disciplinary notions on tectonics, light and comfort, and entire regulatory frameworks. Once designed for and with the human, contemporary interiors have instead become exponentially complex materialisations where the politics of our present moment are played out. Ultimately, who are they for? Titled Interior ecologies, this conference examined the glossaries that characterise contemporary ecology and their implications for interior architecture. From the postmodern concept of sustainability in the 1980s to that of the Anthropocene in the 2000s, and from the contemporary paradigms of the Post-human to the Capitalocene and the Cthulucene in the 2010s, a series of lectures and round tables explored the entanglements between interior spaces, environments and media through successive decentralisations: from the old totalitarianisms that humans have built amongst themselves for centuries (inclusivity) to their position in relation to non-humans (ecology), and finally their relation to machines and their outputs, both real and virtual (technology). Interior Ecologies calls for a vision where the non-human will be central, empowering the agency of traditionally obliterated actors. This involves not only solutions to environmental challenges, but above all the study of the ecosystemic relations between non-living and living organisms (including humans) as crucial for the discipline of interior architecture.
